analysis.one_liner: Sets the federal corporate income tax rate to zero percent.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have set the corporate income tax rate at 0%, died in committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the tax code so that corporations pay 0% of their taxable income in federal income tax, and it would also eliminate the corporate alternative minimum tax, a parallel tax designed to ensure profitable corporations pay at least some tax [S2][S3]. The change would have applied to tax years starting after 2011 [S3]. No offsetting revenue was included, so the roughly $250 billion or more the corporate tax collects each year would simply disappear from federal income [S2]. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders. Setting the tax rate to 0% means every dollar of corporate profit now subject to the 35% federal rate would become tax-free, saving large corporations tens of billions of dollars a year and eliminating the corporate alternative minimum tax [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code to impose a tax of 'zero percent of taxable income' on corporations, eliminating the entire 35% federal corporate income tax [S3].

It also eliminates the corporate alternative minimum tax by setting the corporate tentative minimum tax to zero, freeing corporations from the parallel tax meant to guarantee profitable companies pay some minimum amount [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary taxpayers and anyone who relies on federal programs. With no revenue replacement, the lost corporate tax receipts — historically hundreds of billions of dollars per year — would have to be made up through higher deficits, higher taxes on individuals, or cuts to federal spending [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no replacement revenue, so eliminating the corporate income tax would sharply increase federal deficits or require raising taxes on individuals and cutting spending to compensate [S2][S3].

Because the corporate tax falls heavily on returns to capital, its elimination would disproportionately benefit wealthy households and shareholders rather than working people, while shifting the cost of government onto them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a full windfall to corporate shareholders with no offset and no direct benefit to working people. The cost — hundreds of billions in lost annual revenue — would land on ordinary taxpayers through deficits, higher individual taxes, or cuts to public programs. Supporters argued ending the corporate tax would attract investment and jobs, but the bill included no mechanism to guarantee that, and the unpaid-for revenue loss is by far its dominant feature [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Louie Gohmert introduced the bill on September 14, 2011, with five Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The committee never acted on the bill; the complete action history shows only the introduction and the referral, with no markup, no vote, and no consideration on the House floor [S5].
The bill expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers, since federal revenue from the corporate tax was preserved. No corporations gained, because the bill never became law.

for.name: Rep. Louie Gohmert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set the corporate income tax rate to 0% and eliminate the corporate alternative minimum tax.

for.name: Reps. Michael Burgess, Mike Ross, John Mica, and Blake Farenthold
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, never holding a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill received no action in a committee controlled by the same party [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the entire 35% federal corporate income tax and the corporate alternative minimum tax, a multi-hundred-billion-dollar annual windfall with no offsetting revenue [S2][S3]. The cost would fall on ordinary taxpayers through deficits or higher taxes elsewhere [S2].
